question_text: Identify X and Y. In the show X, the character walks into the Office as he starts his new position. question_text: Identify X and Y. X and Y (a seminal masterpiece) are deeply intertwined. X serves as both a grand visual homage and a spiritual companion to Y, channeling its melancholic soul, aesthetic style, and tragic exploration of the Golden Age. Y was the nation's first CinemaScope film. It revolutionized screen lighting through its signature use of chiaroscuro (high-contrast light and shadow), silhouetted camera operators, and dramatic shafts of natural sunlight piercing through dusty studio rafters. In X, the cinematographer intentionally recreates this exact visual grammar, frequently framing characters inside vast, dimly lit soundstages illuminated by solitary spotlights, capturing dust motes, carbon-arc projector beams, and camera silhouettes as a direct nod to Y. Both X and Y are about the mechanics and tragedy of the film industry itself.
answer_text: X - Jubilee. Y - Kagaz Ke Phool.

question_text: Identify the movie, and explain the logic (funda). The acting credits shown are: A - Andrew Wyke, B - Milo Tindle, Alec Cawthorne - Inspector Doppler*, John Matthews - Detective Sergeant Tarrant, Teddy Martin - Constable Higgins, Eve Channing - Marguerite Wyke.
answer_text: Sleuth. These are fake acting credits - the story hinges heavily on elaborate disguises, fake identities, and mind games, so listing only the two real lead actors (Laurence Olivier and Michael Caine) in the credits would have ruined the mystery for the audience, since viewers would instantly realize that later characters, like the mysterious Inspector Doppler investigating a murder, were played by Michael Caine's character.

question_text: Identify X and Y. X, directed by legendary fight choreographer Lau Kar-leung and produced by the Shaw Brothers, is widely regarded as one of the greatest kung fu films ever made. It catapulted Gordon Liu (Liu Chia-hui) to international stardom and established the blueprint for the martial arts 'training montage'. Gordon Liu plays San Te (based on the legendary historical monk San De); determined to learn kung fu to fight back against tyranny, he spends years grinding through the temple's grueling chambers, each designed to hone a specific physical skill. One of the film's most iconic moments comes during San Te's training in the weapons chamber: when sparring against the Chief Monk, San Te's traditional wooden staff keeps getting trapped and disarmed by the Chief Monk's dual broadswords. Realizing he needs a weapon that combines the defensive reach of a long staff with the flexible, unpredictable angles of a chain whip, San Te invents the sanjiegun (commonly known as Y) by linking short wooden poles together with metal chain rings. Using the flexible strikes, sudden whip attacks, and unique blocking capabilities of Y, San Te successfully counters the dual swords and passes the chamber's ultimate test.
answer_text: X - The 36th Chamber of Shaolin. Y - Three-section staff (3-section staff).

question_text: Identify X. It is a popular myth that if a tree is too large to chop down with an axe, villagers in the Solomon Islands surround the tree every morning and scream, curse, and yell insults at it. After about 30 days of continuous verbal abuse, the tree's spirit dies, its leaves wither, and it falls over on its own. The story was popularized in Western culture by author Robert Fulghum in his 1991 book, 'Uh-Oh: Some Observations from Both Sides of the Refrigerator Door'. This myth was used in X to deliver a blunt warning about the impacts of the emotional abuse of constant disapproval, unrealistic expectations, and harsh criticism.
answer_text: Taare Zameen Par (released internationally as Like Stars on Earth).

question_text: Identify X (4) and A, B, C (2 each). In the universe of X, humanity is divided into three distinct socio-political factions, A, B and C. The divide isn't just political or cultural - centuries of living in different environments have literally altered human anatomy, creating deep-seated tribalism and resentment between them. Faction A: home environment is Earth (abundant natural air, water, and biosphere); physical traits are heavy bone density, compact, robust muscle mass; culturally comfortable but overcrowded, many rely on government welfare; language is a highly clinical, standardized form of English. Faction B: home environment is Mars (enclosed domes, sterile and engineered landscapes); physically slightly taller than A, reliant on military training and drugs to survive 1G; culturally hyper-disciplined, collective, intensely focused on transforming the environment; language is generally standard English with a distinct linguistic quirk from their history of colonization. Faction C: home environment is the asteroid belt (scarce, tightly rationed air and water); physically elongated limbs, thin frames, weaker bone density, use sign language; culturally an exploited blue-collar working class, fiercely independent and tribal; their language is primarily based on English but heavily borrows roots and words from Mandarin Chinese, Spanish, German, Russian, Japanese, French, Portuguese, and Arabic (e.g., Beltalowda, Welwala = traitor who sided with A/B, Owkwa = Water).
answer_text: X - The Expanse. A - Earthers. B - Martians. C - Belters.

question_text: Identify X. X, directed by Gareth Evans, is widely celebrated as one of the greatest, most influential action movies of the 21st century. It introduced global audiences to the brutal martial art of Silat. Before filming, director Gareth Evans required the actors to undergo an intensive boot camp with KOPASKA (Indonesian special forces). Unlike soft or flowy martial arts, the style of Silat shown in X is ruthless, close-quarters, and utilitarian - it emphasizes rapid strikes, bone-breaking joint locks, sweeping takedowns, elbow/knee strikes, and utilizing everyday objects (walls, doorframes, fluorescent light tubes) as improvised weapons. When the SWAT team runs out of ammunition, the film smoothly transitions from tactical gunfights to pure, visceral Silat hand-to-hand combat.

question_text: Whose final work (uncredited)? Legendary sound designer Ben Burtt revealed that the character Garindan, played on-screen by Sadie Eddon in Star Wars: A New Hope, is actually voiced by legendary actor X, famous for his lawman/western roles. Unfortunately, this doesn't mean X actually sauntered into a sound booth and recorded some odd squeaky sounds as a favor to George Lucas - Burtt only discovered years later, after digging through his old notes and tapes, that Garindan's voice was 'an electronic buzzing which had come off of my synthesizer that was triggered by a human voice.' Burtt then realized that this voice belonged to none other than X: the recording was a stock dialogue loop of X's western movies taken directly from the 20th Century Fox sound archives. Burtt added that Garindan's voice 'was triggered by some dialogue like "All right, what are you doin' in this town," or something like that.'
answer_text: John Wayne.
